meta.title: Harmony & Voice Leading: Why Chords Move

plan.title: Harmony & Voice Leading: Why Chords Move
plan.hook: A chord progression isn't a list of chords; it's four melodies that have agreed to travel together.
objectives: Build any triad or seventh chord in any key, in any inversion, and name it from its spelled notes.
Read a progression in Roman numerals and explain what each chord is doing functionally.
Write four-part harmony that resolves tendency tones and avoids the classic faults.
Use ii-V-I, the descending-fifths sequence, borrowed chords, and secondary dominants deliberately.
Harmonise a given melody end to end: choose the chords, set the harmonic rhythm, and voice the parts.
prerequisites: The solfege course (or equivalent): movable Do, scale construction, and intervals
Key signatures and the circle of fifths

sections.heading: Chords as Stacks
points: Triads as stacked thirds: major, minor, diminished, augmented
Seventh chords: major, dominant, minor, half- and fully diminished
Inversions and what the bass note changes
Figured bass: 5/3, 6, 6/4 and the seventh-chord figures
Roman numerals: quality and inversion in one symbol

sections.heading: Function
points: Tonic, subdominant, and dominant as jobs, not names
Tendency tones: why 7 pulls to 1 and 4 pulls to 3
The cadence family: perfect, plagal, interrupted, imperfect
Cadences as punctuation: commas, full stops, and swerves
The cadential six-four: a tonic costume on a dominant job

sections.heading: Voice Leading Rules and Why They Exist
points: Four independent lines: the SATB model and spacing
Parallel fifths and octaves: two voices fusing into one
Doubling rules and the leading tone's special status
Tendency tones must resolve: leading tone up, chordal seventh down
Common tones, contrary motion, and smooth melodic lines

sections.heading: The Progression Toolkit
points: ii-V-I: the engine of tonal harmony
The descending-fifths sequence and how to enter and leave it
Secondary dominants: borrowing V's push for other chords
Borrowed chords from the parallel minor: iv, flat-VI, flat-III
The same shapes in pop dress: I-V-vi-IV and the four-chord loop

sections.heading: Harmonising a Melody
points: Step one: mark the chord tones on the strong beats
Setting the harmonic rhythm: how often chords change
A worked phrase in C major, harmonised end to end
Voicing the result in four parts and checking the joins
Variations: swapping ii for IV, and the cadential six-four ending

sections.heading: Chords as Stacks
sections.body:
You already know how to build a scale and measure an interval. A chord is what happens when you stack those intervals on purpose. Take any note as a root and pile thirds on top of it: root, third, fifth. That three-note stack is a triad, and its flavour is set entirely by the two thirds you chose. A major third under a minor third gives a major triad (C–E–G). Swap the order — minor third below, major third above — and the same outer frame turns minor (D–F–A). Shrink both thirds and the fifth sags to a diminished fifth: B–D–F is diminished. Stretch both and you get augmented, a chord tonal music uses as a spice rather than a home. Four triad types, all from one recipe: thirds, stacked.

Add one more third and the stack becomes a seventh chord, and now the quality of that top interval matters as much as the triad underneath. C–E–G–B is a major seventh chord, smooth and settled. G–B–D–F is a dominant seventh: a major triad carrying a minor seventh, and that small friction is the engine of half the harmony in this course. D–F–A–C is a minor seventh. B–D–F–A is half-diminished, and B–D–F–Ab fully diminished — write those spellings down, because the difference between them is exactly one note and a whole world of behaviour.

A stack can be turned over. The inversion of a chord is decided by one thing only: which note is in the bass. Root in the bass is root position. Third in the bass is first inversion, fifth in the bass is second inversion, and a seventh chord gets a third inversion when its seventh sits in the bass. The notes do not change; the job does. A root-position tonic sounds planted. Put the third in the bass and the same chord leans forward, happy to move. Put the fifth in the bass and it turns unstable, almost a decoration of whatever chord follows — which is why second-inversion triads are rationed in strict writing, reserved for cadences, passing motion, and pedal points.

Figured bass is the old shorthand for all of this, and it is worth reading fluently because harmony books still speak it. The figures count intervals above the bass. Root position is 5/3 — a fifth and a third above the bass — usually written as nothing at all. First inversion is 6/3, abbreviated to 6. Second inversion is 6/4. Seventh chords follow the same logic as they turn over: 7, then 6/5, then 4/3, then 4/2. Roman numerals absorb the whole system into one symbol: the numeral gives the scale degree of the root and the chord's quality (uppercase major, lowercase minor, ° diminished), and the figures ride along as a superscript. I6 means a tonic chord with its third in the bass. V4/3 means a dominant seventh with its fifth in the bass. Once you can read those two symbols without translating, you can read a progression at sight — which is the next skill this course builds, because a stack by itself says nothing about where it wants to go.

questions.q: What is the only thing that decides a chord's inversion?
questions.answer: Which chord note is in the bass: root, third, fifth, or (for seventh chords) the seventh.
questions.hint: The notes in the stack stay the same — one voice's assignment changes.

questions.q: Spell a dominant seventh chord on G, and say which interval makes it 'dominant' rather than major.
questions.answer: G–B–D–F. The seventh above the root is minor (G to F), where a major seventh chord would have F sharp.
questions.hint: Major triad on the bottom, then ask how far the top note sits from the root.

sections.heading: Function
sections.body:
A Roman numeral tells you what a chord is. Function tells you what it is doing. In a major key every diatonic chord falls into one of three jobs. Tonic chords — I, and its stand-ins vi and iii — are places of rest; a phrase can end on them and feel finished. Dominant chords — V and vii° — carry tension that demands release. Subdominant chords — IV and ii — live in between: they leave home without yet raising the stakes. (Many modern books call this middle job predominant, because it usually comes before the dominant; it is the same chair with a different nameplate.) A typical phrase is a round trip: tonic, out to subdominant, up onto dominant, and home. Thousands of pieces are that trip with different scenery.

The tension is not mysterious. It is built out of tendency tones — scale degrees with a strong directional pull. Degree 7, the leading tone, sits a semitone under the tonic and leans up into it; that is why V and vii°, the two chords containing 7, feel like a held breath. Degree 4 leans down to 3, which is why the seventh of a V7 chord — in C major, the F in G–B–D–F — slides down to E when the chord resolves. When you voice-lead well, you are mostly honouring these two pulls and letting everything else take the shortest path. Function is just the name we give to the combined effect: a dominant chord is any chord that makes the ear predict tonic next.

Cadences are where functions meet at a phrase boundary, and they work like punctuation. A perfect cadence, V–I, is the full stop: dominant tension discharged straight into tonic rest, both chords in root position for maximum finality. A plagal cadence, IV–I, is the 'Amen' of hymn singing — gentler, a settling rather than a conclusion. An interrupted cadence, V–vi, sets up the full stop and swerves: the ear expects tonic and gets its substitute, so the phrase has to keep going. An imperfect cadence ends a phrase on V — or reaches V from somewhere — and hangs in the air like a comma: clearly a joint in the music, clearly not the end. Learn to hear these four and you can feel the sentence structure of a piece without counting a single bar.

One impostor deserves its own warning. At a cadence you will often meet I6/4 — a tonic chord in second inversion, fifth in the bass — sitting directly before V. Despite its label it does not behave as tonic at all. Its bass is the dominant scale degree, it arrives on a strong beat, and it leans entirely on the V that follows. Treat it as part of the dominant: I6/4–V–I is one gesture, an accented wind-up and release, and in figured-bass terms the six-four resolves down to 5/3 over the same bass note. Mislabelling it as a resting tonic is the most common reading error in first-year harmony, and now you will not make it.

questions.q: In C major, which two scale degrees are the strongest tendency tones in a V7 chord, and where does each want to go?
questions.answer: Degree 7 (B, the chord's third) pulls up to the tonic C; degree 4 (F, the chord's seventh) pulls down to E.
questions.hint: One sits a semitone below the tonic; the other is the note that makes V7 different from V.

questions.q: A phrase ends with IV moving to I. Name the cadence and its usual nickname.
questions.answer: A plagal cadence — the 'Amen' cadence, from its use at the end of hymns.
questions.hint: Subdominant straight to tonic, no dominant involved.

sections.heading: Voice Leading Rules and Why They Exist
sections.body:
Strip a choir texture down and you find the model underneath all tonal harmony: four voices — soprano, alto, tenor, bass — each singing its own line. The bass has special duties (it defines inversions and roots), but the other three are melodies first and chord-fill second. That is the whole secret of voice leading. A progression is not blocks landing one after another; it is four singers who each need a singable path. Every rule in this section exists to protect that independence, and each one stops making sense the moment you forget it.

Start with the famous prohibition: no parallel fifths or octaves. If two voices stand a perfect fifth apart and both move to another perfect fifth, they have stopped sounding like two voices. The perfect fifth and octave are so acoustically fused — the upper note is nearly a component of the lower one's sound — that moving them in lockstep merges the lines into a single thickened melody, and the four-voice texture quietly becomes three. That is the entire reason for the rule. It is not etiquette and it is not superstition; it is bookkeeping for the ear. (It is also style-specific: rock guitar lives on parallel fifths and calls them power chords, where one fat line is exactly the point. In SATB writing, independence is the point.)

Doubling follows from the same thinking. In a root-position triad, double the root first: it is the chord's most stable note and two voices on it costs nothing. Double the bass in inversions. But never double a tendency tone. The leading tone doubled means two voices both obliged to resolve up to the tonic, and when they do, they arrive in parallel octaves — the fault you were avoiding, produced by a shortcut two chords earlier. A doubled chordal third is sometimes acceptable in minor chords; an incomplete chord — fifth omitted, root tripled — is a standard fix when the alternative is a worse fault.

Resolution rules are the tendency tones from Section 2 with their sleeves rolled up. The leading tone in an outer voice resolves up to the tonic. The seventh of a seventh chord resolves down by step, always: the F of G7 falls to E in the tonic chord, and if your voicing makes that awkward, change the voicing, not the rule. Chord members that can stay, stay — a note common to both chords is held in the same voice, which is why ii and V7 in C major keep their D parked in one voice. Prefer step motion to leaps, contrary motion to similar, and keep the upper three voices within an octave of their neighbours. Follow just these habits and most first-attempt faults vanish, because they were never really about chords. They were about asking one singer to be in two places at once.

questions.q: Why, acoustically, do parallel perfect fifths damage a four-part texture?
questions.answer: A perfect fifth is so fused with its lower note that two voices moving fifth-to-fifth merge into one thickened line, and the texture loses a voice.
questions.hint: It is not about the sound being ugly — it is about how many independent lines the ear can count.

questions.q: The seventh of a dominant seventh chord must do what when the chord resolves?
questions.answer: Resolve down by step — in C major, the F of G7 falls to the E of the tonic chord.
questions.hint: It is a tendency tone, and its tendency is downward.

sections.heading: The Progression Toolkit
sections.body:
A handful of progressions do most of the work in tonal music. Learn them as physical shapes — root motions you can feel — and you will start recognising them everywhere, in every style.

The first is ii–V–I. In C major: Dm7, G7, Cmaj7. Look at the roots — D, G, C — each falling a fifth, sliding down the same chute as Section 2's function journey, with ii doing the subdominant job in its smoothest form. The voice leading is nearly automatic: the seventh of Dm7 (C) is already the tonic note waiting at the end, the seventh of G7 (F) falls to E, and the leading tone B climbs to C. Jazz musicians play this progression in every key, in major and minor, thousands of times a year; classical phrases end with it; pop songs borrow its back half. If you learn one shape cold, learn this one.

Stretch that chute and you get the descending-fifths sequence: I–IV–vii°–iii–vi–ii–V–I, every root a fifth below the last, the whole key laid out as one long slide home. Pachelbel built a canon on a close cousin of it. Baroque ground basses and classical allegro themes alike run on versions of the same staircase. Sequences are how harmony travels — through keys, down the staircase, one predictable step at a time — and the skill is in the joins: enter on a strong chord, keep the pattern for at least two full steps so the ear locks in, and leave through V–I so the arrival feels earned rather than merely stopped.

Two tools break the diatonic frame on purpose. A secondary dominant borrows the dominant's push and aims it at a chord other than tonic: in C major, D major (D–F sharp–A) is not in the key, but placed before G it behaves as V of V — written V/V — and the G arrives with extra inevitability. Any major or minor chord in the key can be tonicised this way. Borrowed chords come from the parallel minor instead: in C major, F minor (F–Ab–C) is iv imported from C minor, darker than the diatonic IV and unmistakable once heard; flat-VI and flat-III travel with it. Film music and rock harmony run on these imports.

Finally, notice that pop wears the same shapes with the labels changed. The four-chord loop I–V–vi–IV — in G major, G, D, Em, C — is a tonic, a dominant push, the tonic substitute, and a subdominant, cycling without a full stop so the song can ride it indefinitely. Verse-chorus harmony is function with the cadence deliberately left open. Nothing in this section is a different system from Sections 2 and 3. It is the same three jobs, the same tendency tones, wearing faster clothes.

questions.q: In C major, a D major chord (D–F sharp–A) appears just before G7. What is it, in Roman numerals with a slash?
questions.answer: V/V — a secondary dominant: the dominant of the dominant, tonicising G for one chord.
questions.hint: Ask which chord it resolves to, then ask what dominant that chord would have.

questions.q: Spell ii–V–I in C major using seventh chords throughout.
questions.hint: All three are diatonic to C major — no accidentals needed anywhere.

sections.heading: Harmonising a Melody
sections.body:
Everything so far assembles here. You are given a melody and nothing else; your job is chords, rhythm, and voices, in that order of thinking but one pass of work. Take this four-bar phrase in C major, one bar per line: C E G E | A G F E | D F G B | C, held for the whole last bar.

Step one is to sort the melody notes into chord tones and travellers. On the strong beats, ask which triad owns the note. Bar 1 is easy: C, E and G are the tonic triad itself, with the second E a return, so the bar is I from top to bottom. Bar 2 opens on A and closes through F and E. A and F belong to two chords — IV (F–A–C) and ii (D–F–A) — while G and E fit neither and are passing notes, travellers between chord tones. Hold both candidates and keep reading. Bar 3 runs D, F, G, B: D, F and B are three of the four notes of G7, and the G is its root passing through. Bar 4 is the arrival: C alone, tonic, end of phrase. So the skeleton is already visible — I, something in the subdominant family, G7, I — and the only real choice is bar 2.

Step two is harmonic rhythm: how often the chord changes. One chord per bar suits this phrase; the melody's own pace says so, and the beginner's error is to demand a new chord for every note, passing tones included, which produces a lurching mess. Choose ii for bar 2 — Dm — because it feeds G7 by the descending-fifth root motion from Section 4, making the whole phrase I–ii–V7–I, the toolkit's central shape. (IV would also work; hold that thought for the variations.) Step three is voicing. Set the melody as the soprano. Keep the joins lazy in the technical sense: between I and ii, move each voice the shortest distance; between ii and G7, hold the shared D in one voice; at the final join, honour the two resolutions — the F of G7 steps down to E, the B steps up to C, and the tritone between them collapses inward onto the tonic chord's root and third. Check the joins against Section 3: no parallel fifths or octaves, no doubled leading tone, spacing sane. The phrase harmonises itself once the decisions are made in the right order.

Variations are where harmonising becomes arranging. Swap bar 2's ii for IV and the phrase brightens — same melody, both readings legal, a different weather. Or strengthen the ending: replace the plain approach to bar 4 with a cadential six-four, so bars 3–4 read I6/4–V7–I and the arrival gets its wind-up from Section 2. Or slow the harmonic rhythm, holding I across bars 1–2 by treating bar 2's A and F as neighbour notes over a tonic pedal. Each variation is a decision you can defend from the rules, which is the difference between harmonising and guessing: the rules do not pick the chord for you, they tell you what each candidate will cost and what it will pay.

questions.q: In bar 2 of the worked phrase (A G F E), why do G and E not need chords of their own?
questions.answer: They are passing notes between the chord tones A and F; the harmonic rhythm stays at one chord per bar, and travellers pass through the prevailing harmony.
questions.hint: Not every melody note is a chord tone — some are just on their way between two that are.

questions.q: State the full progression of the worked example and the two resolutions at its final join.
questions.answer: I–ii–V7–I in C major. At G7–I, F resolves down to E and B resolves up to C.
questions.hint: Bar 2 chose the descending-fifth route into the dominant; the final join is the tritone collapsing.

questions.q: The notes D–F–A–C, stacked in that order, form which chord?
questions.explain: Root D, minor third F, perfect fifth A, minor seventh C: that is a minor seventh chord, Dm7. D7 would need F sharp; Dmaj7 would need C sharp; the stack is rooted on D, not F.

questions.q: In C major, the chord spelled E–G–B is:
questions.explain: E to G is a minor third and E to B a perfect fifth, so the chord is E minor. Built on scale degree 3 in C major, it is iii.

questions.q: Figured bass '6' written under a bass note, with nothing else, most commonly means:
choices: Add a sixth above the bass and stop
questions.explain: '6' abbreviates 6/3: a sixth and a third above the bass, which places the triad's third in the bass — first inversion. Second inversion is 6/4.

questions.q: A hymn phrase in F major ends with B flat major moving to F major. That is:
questions.explain: In F major, B flat is IV and F is I. IV–I is the plagal cadence, the 'Amen' ending — no dominant chord is involved.

questions.q: In A major, a phrase closes E major to F sharp minor. Name the cadence.
questions.explain: E major is V in A major and F sharp minor is vi. V–vi swerves away from the expected tonic, so the phrase must continue: an interrupted cadence.

questions.q: Why does a dominant chord create such a strong expectation of the tonic?
choices: Because it is always the loudest chord in the phrase
Because it contains the leading tone, a semitone below the tonic, and often degree 4 leaning down to 3
Because it is built only from notes outside the scale
Because tradition forbids ending a phrase anywhere else
questions.explain: V contains scale degree 7, which pulls up to 1, and V7 adds degree 4, which pulls down to 3. The expectation is in the notes themselves, not in volume or convention.

questions.q: In strict four-part writing, parallel perfect fifths between two voices are avoided mainly because:
choices: They sound harsh and dissonant to modern ears
They break the rule that all voices must move by step
The two voices fuse into one line, so the texture loses an independent part
They can only be written with forbidden doubled notes
questions.explain: A perfect fifth is acoustically fused with its lower note. Two voices travelling fifth-to-fifth merge into a single thickened line, and four-part writing becomes three-part writing by accident.

questions.q: A student's I–V progression in C major has bass C moving to G while the tenor moves G up to D. What is the fault?
choices: Parallel perfect fifths between bass and tenor
Parallel octaves between bass and tenor
questions.explain: Bass and tenor stand a fifth apart (C–G) and move in the same direction to another fifth (G–D): consecutive perfect fifths. The interval is a fifth both times, not an octave, and there is no seventh chord or leading tone involved.

questions.q: In G major, V7 is D7 (D–F sharp–A–C). Its chordal seventh, C, must:
choices: Resolve up by step to D
Be doubled so the resolution is stronger
Leap down to the bass note
Resolve down by step to B
questions.explain: A chordal seventh always resolves down by step. In the move D7 to G, the C falls to B, the third of the tonic chord.

questions.q: In C major, which progression is a descending-fifths sequence?
choices: C – F – B° – Em – Am – Dm – G – C
questions.explain: Each root falls a fifth from the one before: C to F to B to E to A to D to G to C. The other options mix whole-step and third root motions.

questions.q: In C major, an F minor chord (F–A flat–C) appears in an otherwise diatonic passage. It is best explained as:
choices: A borrowed chord — iv from the parallel minor
questions.explain: F minor is the subdominant chord of C minor, the parallel minor. Imported into C major it is written iv, a standard borrowed chord. A single borrowed chord colours the key without modulating.

questions.q: Spell a ii–V–I in G major, triads only.
questions.explain: In G major, ii is A minor (A–C–E), V is D major (D–F sharp–A), and I is G major (G–B–D). The roots fall in fifths: A, D, G.

questions.q: The first step in harmonising an unfamiliar melody is to:
choices: Choose a chord for every note, including passing tones
Decide the final cadence and work backwards only
Mark the strong-beat notes and identify which chords own them as chord tones
Pick the most colourful borrowed chords available
questions.explain: Strong beats carry the harmony. Sorting chord tones from passing and neighbour notes first reveals the phrase's skeleton; chords for every note produces lurching, over-busy harmony.

questions.q: In bar 3 of the worked example, the melody runs D–F–G–B over G7. The F is:
choices: A passing note with no chord status
The chordal seventh, which must resolve down to E at the tonic
A borrowed note from the parallel minor
questions.explain: G7 is G–B–D–F, so F is its seventh. At the join to I it resolves down by step to E, exactly as Section 3 requires.

questions.q: A student voices the final G7–I join with the B (leading tone) placed in two voices at once. Why is that a fault waiting to happen?
choices: The leading tone may never appear in an inner voice
Two leading tones must both resolve up to C, producing parallel octaves
B is not a member of the tonic chord
Seventh chords may not contain the leading tone
questions.explain: A doubled tendency tone doubles its obligation. Both Bs resolve up to C, and the two voices land an octave apart having moved in parallel — the classic hidden cost of doubling the leading tone.

sections.title: Chords as Stacks
bullets: A triad is two stacked thirds: root, third, fifth.
Third order sets the type: major, minor, diminished, augmented.
One more third makes a seventh chord — dominant 7th is a major triad plus a minor seventh.
Inversion is decided by the bass note alone.
Figured bass: 5/3 root position, 6 first inversion, 6/4 second inversion; sevenths run 7, 6/5, 4/3, 4/2.
sections.notes: Open with the stack, not the symbol. Spell C–E–G, then G–B–D–F, and let the class hear that the second stack has a rub in it. Inversions come next: same notes, new bass, new behaviour. Finish on the symbols — once I6 and V4/3 read instantly, the rest of the course gets much faster.
sections.visual: Keyboard with C, E and G highlighted beside the stacked-thirds diagram from the reading.

sections.title: Function
bullets: Three jobs: tonic (rest), subdominant (departure), dominant (tension).
Tendency tones drive the system: 7 pulls to 1, 4 pulls to 3.
Perfect V–I is the full stop; plagal IV–I is the Amen.
Interrupted V–vi swerves; imperfect cadences hang on V like a comma.
Cadential I6/4 is dominant function wearing a tonic label.
sections.notes: Play or sing the four cadences back to back before naming them — the punctuation metaphor lands once the ears have voted. The cadential six-four needs a slow pass: same tonic notes, dominant job, because the bass and the beat say so.
sections.visual: The three-function map with the T–SD–D–T journey and the four cadences listed as punctuation.

sections.title: Voice Leading Rules and Why They Exist
bullets: Four voices, four melodies: SATB parts are lines first, chord-fill second.
Parallel fifths and octaves fuse two voices into one — that is the whole objection.
Double the root; double the bass in inversions; never double a tendency tone.
Leading tone resolves up; the chordal seventh resolves down by step.
Keep common tones in the same voice; prefer step and contrary motion.
sections.notes: Teach every rule as a repair for a specific accident. Parallels: two singers became one. Doubled leading tone: two singers owe the same resolution and collide in octaves. Seventh left hanging: a tendency tone broke its promise. When the class can name the accident, they stop needing the rule list.
sections.visual: The four-part I–V example in open score, tenor common tone marked, from the reading.

sections.title: The Progression Toolkit
bullets: ii–V–I: roots fall in fifths; the voice leading nearly does itself.
The descending-fifths sequence tours the whole key: I–IV–vii°–iii–vi–ii–V–I.
Secondary dominants borrow V's push: V/V in C major is D major.
Borrowed chords import parallel-minor colour: iv, flat-VI, flat-III.
Pop's I–V–vi–IV loop is the same three functions with the cadence left open.
sections.notes: Work the toolkit at the keyboard if one is handy. ii–V–I in C, then in G, then in F — the shape should become a hand position, not a calculation. End with the four-chord pop loop and ask the class to name each chord's function; it demystifies a thousand songs at once.
sections.visual: The descending-fifths root-motion diagram: eight chords linked by down-a-fifth arrows.

sections.title: Harmonising a Melody
bullets: Step one: sort melody notes into chord tones and travellers on the strong beats.
Set the harmonic rhythm before choosing chords — one chord per bar here.
The worked phrase: I–ii–V7–I in C major, chosen for its fifth-driven root motion.
Voice the joins lazily: hold common tones, resolve F to E and B to C.
Variations: ii swapped for IV, a cadential six-four ending, or a tonic pedal.
sections.notes: Do the worked phrase slowly, out loud, decision by decision: what owns this note, how often do chords change, which candidate feeds the dominant best. Then play the two variations and let the class argue for one. That argument — with rules as evidence — is the course's real final exercise.
sections.visual: The four-bar worked-example chart: melody notes over each bar, chosen chord beneath, tritone resolution marked.

enrichment.audioTitle: Harmonising a Phrase, Live: One Proposal, One Objection at a Time

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: Here is a bare melody in C major, four bars: C E G E, then A G F E, then D F G B, then a long C. Harmonise it. Where do you start?

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: I'd give every note its own chord. C major under the C, then something under the E, something under the G...

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: And that is objection number one. The G in bar two and the E after it are not chord tones — they are travellers walking between A and F. One chord per bar. Let the travellers pass through it.

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: All right, one per bar. Bar one is obviously C major — the melody is the chord. Bar two: A and F... that's F major or D minor.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: Both legal. Before you pick, look at bar three: D, F, G, B. What owns three of those four notes?

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: G7. D, F and B are in it, and the G is its root just passing through. So bar three is G7, and bar four is the tonic.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: Now choose bar two with bar three in mind. F major or D minor — which one feeds G7 better?

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: D minor. Its root falls a fifth into G, so the whole thing runs I, ii, V7, I — the descending-fifth chute.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: Agreed. Now voice the final join. Your G7 has an F in the alto. Where does it go?

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: Down to E, it's the chordal seventh. And the B — leading tone — climbs to C. The tritone just collapses inward.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: Good. Now I will be difficult: put the leading tone in the soprano AND the tenor for a fuller sound. What breaks?

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: Both Bs have to resolve up to C, so the two voices land in octaves — I have written parallel octaves into my own resolution. No doubling the leading tone.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: Exactly. One more liberty: swap bar two to F major. Is the phrase ruined?

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: No — it still works, it's just brighter and less driven. ii pulls toward the dominant; IV sits more still. It's a taste decision, not a correctness one.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: That sentence is the whole course. The rules tell you what each choice costs; they do not make the choice. Last variation — how do you make the ending feel bigger? And when you use it, label it honestly.

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: Put a cadential six-four in front of the G7, so the ending runs I6/4, V7, I — wind-up, then release. Tonic notes, dominant job — labelled honestly.

nodes.note: Four independent lines: no parallel fifths or octaves, no doubled tendency tones, resolutions honoured.

nodes.label: Progression Toolkit

nodes.label: Tendency Tones
nodes.note: The engine under everything: 7 rises to 1, 4 falls to 3, chordal sevenths resolve down.

mnemonics.aid: Perfect Proclaims the end (V–I), Plagal Prays it (IV–I, the Amen), Interrupted Interrupts (V–vi), Imperfect leaves it Inconclusive (ending on V).
Root position wears no numbers (5/3). A 6 means the third is in the basement; 6/4 means the fifth is in the basement. The figure always describes what sits above the bass.

mnemonics.for: Seventh-chord figured bass as the chord turns over
mnemonics.aid: 7, 6/5, 4/3, 4/2 — the numbers count down as the chord tips over, one inversion at a time, ending with the seventh itself in the bass at 4/2.
